## Study I: Scoping Review Results

The study selection process is summarized in @fig-prisma. The MEDLINE and Embase search resulted in 4884 records screened on title and abstract, and 81 reports were assessed for eligibility based on full-text review by two independent reviewers. The citation search on the included 51 reports identified 2 additional reports, which finally resulted in 53 included reports in total. All included and excluded reports are reported in @sec-suppl-study1-reports.

::: {#fig-prisma fig-scap='Flow diagram of study selection.'}

[![](figures/4_results_fig/study_1_prisma.png)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HeleneThomsen/dissertation/main/figures/4_results_fig/study_1_prisma.svg)

Flow diagram of study selection.\
Reproduced from Thomsen et al.[@Thomsen2026], originally published in JMIR Diabetes, under the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY 4.0).

:::

### Study Populations
The study population most common was people with T2D (34 of studies), then people with T1D (20 of 53) and lastly prediabetes (4 of 53). Most studies included adult participants, whereas seven focused on children younger than 18 years. Two studies included only male participants, whereas the remaining studies included both male and female participants.

The geographic distribution was found based on the hospitals and centers where data was collected or by the first author's affiliation when the other options were not available. The distribution was uneven as shown in  @fig-geographical.
Most studies were conducted in Asia (27 of 53) or Europe (22 of 53). Three studies included data from North America, one was conducted in Australia, and only one included data from an African country, although its study population was predominantly White.[@Borg2011] No data was included from South America (@sec-suppl-geo-map).


::: {#fig-geographical fig-scap='Geographical location of the studies.'}
[![](figures/4_results_fig/study_1_world_map.png)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HeleneThomsen/dissertation/main/figures/4_results_fig/study_1_world_map.png)

Geographical location of the studies. Countries colored in red indicate the geographical locations where the studies were conducted. Figure was created using MapChart [https://www.mapchart.net/](https://www.mapchart.net).

:::

### Study Designs and Demographics
Only one study was a randomized controlled trial,[@Pulkkinen2020] and the remaining studies were observational.
Most studies used a cross-sectional design, with the cardiovascular outcome assessed at the same time as the CGM sensor was given.
Only six studies performed longitudinal analyzes. Study sample sizes varied considerably, ranging from 17[@Hoffman2013] to 6,225[@Lu2021] participants, with a median of 152.
CGM data were obtained either from participants' own devices (11 studies) or from CGM devices provided as part of the study (42 studies). 
Statistical analyzes most commonly included linear regression (22 studies) and logistic regression (22 studies), followed by Spearman or Pearson correlation analyzes (11 studies) and Cox proportional hazards regression (3 studies).
Several studies performed additional exploratory analyzes, such as correlation analyzes, to identify relevant covariates for inclusion in regression models.

All included studies primarily investigated associations between CGM-derived measures and cardiovascular outcomes. Only three studies reported predictive performance measures as part of secondary analyzes,[@Su2011; @Mi2012; @Koroleva2022] and none applied machine learning methods. Furthermore, none of the included studies provided openly available data or source code. Instead, availability was either not addressed or limited to access upon reasonable request from the corresponding author.

### Continuous Glucose Monitoring
Medtronic CGM devices were the most frequently used (28 of 53 studies), followed by Abbott (9 of 53) and Dexcom (5 of 53). Other manufacturers included Menarini, Meiqi Company, and SIBIONICS. Sampling intervals ranged from 3 to 15 minutes but were reported in only a minority of studies (21 of 53).
TIR (22 studies) and MAGE (23 studies) were the most frequently investigated CGM-derived metrics (@tbl-study1-cgm-count).
When stratified by T1D and T2D then TIR was the most frequently investigated metric in T1D populations (10 of 23 studies), whereas MAGE was less commonly investigated (5 of 22 studies). In T2D populations, TIR and MAGE were investigated in 11 of 23 and 14 of 22 studies, respectively. Studies conducted in T2D populations also tended to include larger sample sizes than those in T1D populations (median [IQR]: TIR, 510 [405–600] vs. 214 [119–547]; MAGE, 251 [89–411] vs. 57 [30–215]).

### Prediction Studies
Only three studies evaluated the predictive performance of CGM-derived metrics for cardiovascular outcomes, all using logistic regression models with MAGE as the predictor. Two studies reported \acr{AUROC} values of 0.61 and 0.62, respectively,[@Mi2012; @Su2011] and both found MAGE to outperform HbA1c (\acr{AUROC}: 0.55 and 0.58, respectively). The third study used receiver operating characteristic analyzis to determine the optimal threshold for dichotomizing MAGE during variable selection but did not report the \acr{AUROC}.[@Koroleva2022] Instead, a threshold of MAGE ≥ 3.4 mmol/L was identified as a risk factor for stenosis and/or occlusion, with a sensitivity of 0.60 and a specificity of 0.61.

\newpage

### Clinical Association Studies
Most studies focused exclusively on subclinical cardiovascular outcomes (37 of 53 studies, 70%), whereas 13 studies (25%) investigated only clinical cardiovascular outcomes and three studies (6%) included both clinical and subclinical outcomes. An overview of all the studies is provided in @sec-suppl-subclin-results.

Adjustment for potential confounders varied considerably across studies. Demographic factors were most frequently included (n = 36), followed by medical history and biochemical factors (n = 32 each), anthropometric factors (n = 29), and physiological factors (n = 24). Lifestyle factors were included in 20 studies, whereas adjustment for medication, CGM-derived metrics, and CVD markers was less common. Adjustment was not applicable in 12 studies, and six studies did not report whether or how the analyses were adjusted (@tbl-adjustments). Because studies could adjust for variables from several domains, the categories are not mutually exclusive.

An overview of the most frequently used CGM-derived metrics stratified based on clinical and subclinical cardiovascular outcomes are shown in @tbl-CVD-CGM.
Outcomes related to subclinical cardiovascular outcomes were more frequently studied (59 studies) compared to clinical outcomes (26 studies) and studies were predominantly done among people with T2D.
Among clinical cardiovascular outcomes, coronary artery disease was examined most frequently (6 studies), followed by macrovascular complications (5 studies) and the Gensini score (4 studies) and for subclinical cardiovascular outcomes, particularly arterial wall thickness were frequently investigated (19 studies), arterial stiffness (12 studies), cardiac and pulse-related measures (10 studies), and flow resistance (9 studies). 

TIR was the most commonly reported CGM-derived metric across most arterial-stiffness outcomes, followed by MAGE, MBG, SD, and CV. MAGE was reported most frequently in studies evaluating coronary artery disease, Gensini score, and Syntax score. By contrast, relatively few CGM-derived metrics were reported for mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events, stroke, peripheral artery disease, and lower-extremity arterial disease.
A more detailed extraction table of the CVD outcomes for the 53 studies can be found in @sec-suppl-subclin-results.
